items.summary:
OpenAI announced ten significant results in mathematics and theoretical computer science generated by its internal Astra AI model, which addressed long-standing open problems across areas such as high-dimensional geometry, coding theory, group theory, quantum complexity, and lattice cryptography. These results include disproving the Erdős unit-distance conjecture, establishing the existence of non-sofic groups, and providing new bounds on sphere-packing density and arithmetic circuit complexity.

The AI-generated proofs were formalized and prepared into manuscripts with human assistance, and OpenAI emphasizes transparency in attribution, acknowledging the AI's role in producing the mathematical arguments. The company highlights the importance of broad access to AI tools for researchers and encourages the mathematical community to engage with these findings to advance future research and discovery.

items.originalTitle: Prevent cognitive debt by manually retyping LLM-generated code
items.summary:
A developer describes a workflow where they manually type out code generated by large language models (LLMs) instead of directly copying it, aiming to maintain a thorough understanding of their projects and avoid accumulating cognitive debt. This approach slows down development compared to fully automated code generation but helps build a mental model of the codebase and detect errors or design issues early.

The developer instructs their coding assistant to propose edits and commands in chat rather than applying them automatically, allowing manual review and integration. This method echoes traditional advice to type out code examples to learn effectively and is intended to preserve comprehension over raw productivity. The developer plans to continue this practice to balance the benefits of AI assistance with personal code mastery.

items.title: AirLLM enables inference of 70B parameter LLMs on a single 4GB GPU without quantization or pruning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AirLLM 70B inference with single 4GB GPU
items.summary:
AirLLM is an open-source project that significantly reduces memory usage during inference, allowing large language models with up to 70 billion parameters to run on a single 4GB GPU. It achieves this without relying on quantization, distillation, or pruning techniques, and supports even larger models like Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB and DeepSeek-V3 671B on about 12GB by streaming sparse MoE model experts one at a time.

The project includes features such as model compression for up to 3x inference speed improvements, support for various popular models including Qwen, Baichuan, and Mistral, and compatibility with MacOS. Recent updates have added support for extremely large models like Kimi K3 (2.8 trillion parameters) running on under 4GB of VRAM by loading only the necessary experts per token, requiring specific dependencies and CUDA versions.

items.title: UNAM orders 58,000 students to retake remote AI-proctored entrance exam after widespread cheating concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: An AI-supervised remote exam went so badly that 58,000 students must retake it
items.summary:
Mexico's largest university, UNAM, administered its entrance exam remotely for the first time using AI-powered webcam proctoring and a lockdown browser, but the results showed an unprecedented surge in top scores, raising suspicions of cheating. A commission investigating the irregularities recommended a new in-person "control exam" for all admitted students and those meeting minimum scores since 2021, affecting about 58,000 applicants.

The remote exam, taken by nearly 160,000 applicants, saw 16.3% scoring 100 or more compared to 3.5% in previous years, and 5.5% scoring 110 or more versus 0.9% historically. Despite AI monitoring and human supervisors, cheating methods including use of AI tools off-camera, cheat sheets, and impersonation were reportedly widespread. UNAM's rector apologized to honest students and emphasized the control exam is necessary to ensure fairness and equity in admissions.

items.originalTitle: Trump’s AI protectionism has come for robotics
items.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission, influenced by the Trump administration, has issued a broad ban on importing advanced foreign robots including humanoids, quadrupeds, and wheeled models, citing national security risks and the need to protect US robotics companies from Chinese competition. This move reflects an expansion of AI industry protectionism beyond software to include emerging robotics sectors.

The FTC's decision highlights concerns over data collection by foreign-made robots and aims to foster a stronger domestic supply chain. However, US robotics research heavily relies on affordable Chinese robots, which offer a better price-to-capability ratio than US-made alternatives, raising concerns that the ban could hinder innovation and slow industry growth. The ruling underscores the administration's view of humanoid robotics as a strategic AI frontier worthy of protection despite the sector's current developmental challenges.

items.summary:
Palantir CEO Alex Karp described the AI industry as having 'Marxist overtones' in a shareholder letter following the company's record $1.9 billion revenue and $1.1 billion profit in the second quarter. He criticized AI frontier labs for attempting to control the means of production of their enterprise partners, raising concerns about trust and data ownership.

Karp contrasted Palantir's approach, which offers model-agnostic AI software allowing clients to control their data and AI processes, with AI labs that he said migrate clients' intellectual property to their own models. He framed this as a moral justification by AI companies to dominate enterprises, a view he elaborated on during a conference call with Wall Street analysts. Despite his critique, Palantir's strong financial results reflect growing enterprise adoption of AI technologies.

Pangram was founded in 2023 by AI researchers from Tesla and Google with a mission to rebuild trust in generative AI content.

items.summary:
Over the weekend, Jasjeet Sekhon, the chief strategy officer at Google’s DeepMind AI unit, used two words to describe what needs to happen to justify his industry’s unprecedented capital expenditures: recursive self-improvement. The white-hot term refers to AI that can automatically create better versions of itself.

RSI is a “key part of the investment thesis,” Sekhon said at the Agentic AI Summit, which took place at the University of California-Berkeley.

RSI is the new AGI (artificial general intelligence) in the sense that it’s all anyone in the field is talking about as the industry’s next goalpost. Whether RSI would precede or coincide with AGI—AI that is better than humans at most economically valuable tasks—is an entirely different conversation!

To be fair to Sekhon, RSI has been an industry goal for some time. I first started hearing the term from researchers in early 2023. But it wasn’t part of corporations’ public rhetoric until recent weeks.

items.title: How an Apple iCloud Policy Fueled Employee Leaks Ahead of OpenAI Suit
items.originalTitle: How an Apple iCloud Policy Fueled Employee Leaks Ahead of OpenAI Suit
items.summary:
In a lawsuit early last month, Apple accused former employees who are now at OpenAI of stealing a trove of trade secrets from the iPhone maker—in part by improperly accessing confidential Apple documents after they left the company. Even before the suit was filed, some of the more than 400 former Apple employees who now work at OpenAI began receiving stern letters from Apple lawyers informing them they were in possession of confidential Apple material, people familiar with the matter said.

But the reason many of them had access to that material was due to an Apple policy, not because the former employees were attempting to steal its secrets, the people said. The issue: Even though Apple kicked them off most of its corporate systems after they resigned, the former employees continued to have access to Apple files shared with them when they still worked there.

One of the arguments for open source software for end-users has always been the freedom to examine and modify how that software works.

The reality for most people - even expert programmers - has been that the freedom is more about being able to lean on other people to do that. Most people can't justify the time commitment needed to read and then modify the code for tools they use very often.

I think LLMs have changed that equation in a way that makes the original dream much more feasible.

Several times a day I'll prompt regular Claude chat to "Clone x/y from GitHub and tell me how Z works".

Getting software to compile in order to start hacking on it used to be enough friction that I often wouldn't bother. Now I treat that as a zero time investment challenge: tell Codex or Claude Code to checkout and build X and then come back ten minutes later and see how it got on.

I'm not habitually modifying the software I use yet, but I can see a path to that which didn't exist a year or so ago.
